## **Re: Quality Wind Project – Bird and Bat Monitoring, 2014 Annual Report**

The enclosed report documents our Quality Wind Project bird and bat monitoring for 2014. We have appreciated the opportunity to work with you on this project and trust that this report meets your requirements. Please feel free to contact the undersigned by phone or email regarding any questions or further information that you may require.

## Regards, **Hemmera**

Ashleigh Ballevona, B.Sc. BIT. Biologist 604.831.6231 aballevona@hemmera.com

Charlie Palmer, M.Sc., P.Biol., R.P.Bio. Practice Leader (EIA) 604.669.0424 (125) cpalmer@hemmera.com

## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

The Quality Wind Project Bird and Bat Monitoring Program (Program) was developed to address environmental commitment 5.7.7 of Capital Power Corporation’s Environmental Assessment Certificate (#E10-01, June 2010) for the Quality Wind Project (QWP). The first year of bird and bat fatality monitoring was conducted in 2013 and this report represents the second year of monitoring.

Carcass searches conducted between April and October 2014 recovered 26 bats, the first on April 22, the last on September 30. Bat fatalities peaked during spring and fall migration periods. More migratory tree bats (n=21) were recovered than myotis species (n=5), which is consistent with the 2014 QWP results (Hemmera 2013), and most previous studies; migratory tree bats have been more frequently impacted at wind energy developments (Johnson et al. 2004, Barclay et al. 2007, Arnett et al. 2008, Hein et al., 2013).

After correcting the bat carcass recoveries for searcher efficiency, scavenger removal, and search area biases, we estimated 118 fatalities or 1.5 bats/turbine/year (0.8 bats/MW/year) at the QWP in 2014. With no provincial threshold for bat fatalities in British Columbia, the results were compared to thresholds from Alberta (4 – 8 migratory bats/turbine/year (Alberta Provincial Government 2013)) and Ontario (10 bats/turbine/year (OMNR 2011 _a_ )). Effects on bats from the QWP are below both the Alberta and Ontario thresholds.

After accounting for searcher efficiency, scavenger removal, and search area biases, the 11 birds recovered during carcass searches in 2014 yield a fatality estimate of 78 birds or 1.0 birds/turbine/year (0.6 birds/MW/year). The QWP annual fatality estimate is below the OMNR (2011) threshold of 14 birds/turbine/year, below the national mean of 1.3 fatalities per turbine (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014), below a South Peace regional estimate of 2.2 birds/turbine/year (using data from Bear Mountain Wind and Dokie – two nearby operating wind projects), and below the 2.10 to 3.35 small birds/MW average calculated to be the effect on passerines for North American wind energy facilities (Erikson et al. 2014).

After two years of monitoring, the effects on bats are considered consistent with the low to moderate level of effect predicted in the environmental assessment (EPCOR 2009), and the effects on birds are considered consistent with the low level of effect predicted. No significant residual effects were identified and no additional monitoring is recommended.

## **1.0 INTRODUCTION**

## **1.1 BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE**

The Quality Wind Project Bird and Bat Monitoring Program (the Program, Hemmera 2012) was developed in association with the Ministry of Forest Lands and Natural Resource Operations (MoFLNRO). It outlines the methods to address environmental commitment 5.7.7 of Capital Power Corporation’s Environmental Assessment Certificate (#E10-01, June 2010) for the Quality Wind Project (QWP). Namely:

“The Proponent must develop a fatality monitoring plan for operations for birds and bats, in adherence to Environment Canada (EC) guidelines (Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) 2007). The plan must be completed six months prior to the start of operations for review and comment by the responsible regulatory agencies, and be implemented in the first spring or fall season following commissioning. The monitoring must continue for two years, and at the end of each year the monitoring and mitigation prescribed by the program must be reviewed, revised, and, if necessary, altered by the Proponent and responsible regulatory agencies”.

“The fundamental element of the monitoring and follow-up proposed is a feedback loop whereby monitoring results will be evaluated annually by the Proponent and responsible regulatory agencies to verify the results of the impact assessment, and if inconsistencies are found (i.e., if there are significant residual impacts) further mitigation will be applied. That mitigation will in turn be monitored for its effectiveness, and altered if monitoring results show the need.”

The two year Program is consistent with the Environmental Assessment (EA) application (EPCOR 2009) and relevant portions of Canadian guidance documents (CWS 2007). The Program collects the data required to examine relationships between turbines and fatalities to address the following questions:

- What are the corrected (for searcher bias, scavenger removal and area searched) fatality estimates for birds and bats – thus allowing for comparisons with other wind energy projects operating in North America?

- Are fatalities in the following categories (songbirds, raptors, resident bats, migratory tree bats) distributed evenly among turbines?

- Are any turbines responsible for mass mortality events, suggesting evaluation of, and consideration for, operational mitigation?

- Is the EA Application prediction of effects (non-significant) accurate, and are follow-up actions to reduce effects necessary?

The QWP began commercial operation in November 2012; and as per the commitment, the first year of operational bird and bat monitoring began in spring 2013, and the second year began in spring 2014.

Results will be submitted to the relevant regulatory agencies (Ministry of Forests Lands and Natural Resource Operations, MoFLNRO and the BC Environmental Assessment Office, EAO) through submission of this report. Fatality data will be entered into a joint database (Environment Canada, Canadian Wind Energy Association, Bird Studies Canada, Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources) hosted by Bird Studies Canada (BSC).

## **1.2 PROJECT DESCRIPTION AND STUDY AREA**

The QWP is a 142.2 MW wind energy project located on Crown Land approximately 10 km northeast of Tumbler Ridge, BC. A total of 79 Vestas V90 (n=35) and V100 (n=44) wind turbine generators each with a nameplate output of 1.8 MW are expected to operate for 25 years. All turbines are 95 m tall at the nacelle; the V90s have 44 m blades and the V100s have 49 m blades. Turbine locations are shown in **Figures 1A** and **1B** . Thirty three of the V100 turbines are located in the southern portion of the QWP.

**Figure 1A Turbine locations – north portion of the QWP**

**Figure 1B Turbine locations – south portion of the QWP**

The QWP has an operational footprint of approximately 17 km[2] and is located between 1,080 m and 1,260 m elevation on a raised plateau east of the Murray River (visible in **Figure 1A** and **B** above) near the boundary of the Kiskatinaw Plateau and Hart Foothills Ecosections. The QWP is located in two biogeoclimatic zones, and three subzones: the Bullmoose moist, very cold subzone of the Englemann Spruce Subalpine Fir zone (ESSFmv2) and both the Peace moist warm and Murray wet cool subzones of the Boreal Black and White Spruce zone (BWBSmw1 and BWBSwk1). Only a portion of the transmission line corridor overlaps with the BWBSmw1.

The ESSFmv2, found at higher elevations (950 – 1550 m) than either BWBS subzone, is the most abundant biogeoclimatic subzone in the QWP. The ESSFmv2 is characterized by Engelmann ( _Picea engelmannii_ ) or hybrid spruce and subalpine fir ( _Abies lasiocarpa_ ) in climax forests and lodgepole pine ( _Pinus contorta_ ) and black spruce ( _Picea mariana_ ) at lower elevation with poor soils (DeLong et al. 1994). The BWBSwk1 is typically found from 850 – 1200 m elevation and mature forests are dominated by white spruce ( _Picea glauca_ ) with black spruce often found on wet and poor sites. Lodgepole pine is common as an early seral species as is trembling aspen ( _Populus tremuloides_ ) at lower elevation with warm aspects (DeLong et al. 2011). The BWBSmw is found between 750 and 1050 m with upland forests typically dominated by trembling aspen. Lodegpole pine and white spruce can establish were disturbances (harvesting or fire) are less common. Balsam poplar ( _Populus baslamifera_ ) and white or hybrid spruce are

common on moist upland sites with rich soils. Approximately 40% of the QWP operational footprint was altered by the 2006 Hourglass fire and contains standing dead timber and early successional vegetation.

## **2.0 METHODS**

The methods used for the Program were based on experience monitoring bird and bat fatalities in the Peace Region (particularly Bear Mountain Wind), EC protocols for monitoring bird impacts from wind turbines (CWS 2007), and results and insights provided by existing monitoring reports across North America.

Due to the size of the Project (79 turbines), a subset of 40 turbines representative of the Project area and habitats were selected for twice weekly sampling. The sampled subset included turbines in areas that may provide greater risk to birds, i.e., the ends of turbine arrays, and topographic features such as ridges and peaks. This approach is consistent with (CWS 2007). **Figures 1A** and **1B** above illustrate the turbines selected for sampling. Refer to the _Quality Wind Project Bird and Bat Monitoring Program_ , (Hemmera 2012) for analysis and further details on selection of sampling plot locations.

Search schedules (the order and numbers of turbines searched on consecutive surveys) were designed to reduce observer bias, time of day bias, and location bias. The 40 sampled turbines were divided into four subsets of ten turbines and these subsets were sampled such that northern and southern portions of the QWP were sampled during each event to reduce potential location bias. Field technicians alternated between subsets to reduce searcher bias that could occur if the same searcher was always responsible for a given set of turbines. The order in which the subsets were searched was reversed during each event as a means of reducing the time of day bias. Because scavengers may remove fresh carcasses rapidly, changing the order, and therefore the time of day in which turbines were searched, ensured that all turbines were sampled early in the day at least part of the time reducing the opportunity for scavengers to remove carcasses. Scavenger removal and searcher efficiency trials were conducted to quantify the implications of these biases on fatality estimates ( **Sections 2.2** and **2.3** below).

Each of the 40 search turbines was searched, on average, 51 (SD=10) times between April 3 and October 14, 2014, with substitutions as required for maintenance or weather considerations. Turbine T17 was struck by lightning and did not operate for approximately six weeks and searches were instead conducted on turbine 12 during this time (12 search events). Searches on turbine 5 were hampered by dense vegetation from re-vegetation mitigation activity and rough terrain that made searching ineffective and unsafe. Searches were instead conducted on turbine 5 (28 search events). Turbine 47 was searched instead of turbine 46 due to dense and high re-vegetation growth (28 search events), and once instead of turbines 49 and 50 which were undergoing maintenance (one search event). On 22 occasions nonscheduled turbines were searched due to safety requirements associated with operational maintenance

of turbines that were scheduled for searches. These nearby “substitute” turbines were searched between 1 and 4 times each.

## **2.1 DATA COLLECTION**

The following data, consistent with CWS 2007 were collected during carcass search events:

- Date, start and end time, and search area at each turbine.

- For each carcass the following information and a photograph:

   - Date and time of detection.

   - Condition (intact, scavenged, or feather spot).

   - Estimated date of death (fresh, two days, several days, > week).

   - Extent and type of injury.

   - Species, length, sex and age (where possible).

   - UTM coordinates and distance and direction of nearest turbine (derived from UTM locations).

   - Substrate type.

Data was captured electronically using iPads with GPS / GLONASS capability and synchronised daily with an online database. Surveyors recorded daily track logs of search patterns using an iPad GPS application, the results of which were checked after each event to ensure consistency in search coverage.

Recovered carcasses were photographed in place and then placed in a labelled Ziploc bag marked with date, time, UTM coordinates (i.e., location), species and sex/age, if possible. A unique identification code was written on each bag following the search. All carcasses were stored in an on-site freezer.

Bat species and sex (penis presence / absence) were determined using the identification key from Nagorsen and Brigham (1993), adapted to include eastern red bat ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ). Bats were aged by the absence/presence of swollen digits (Nagorsen and Brigham 1993) and/or pale bands on either side of digit joints indicating incomplete ossification associated with juvenile bats (Hutson and Racey 2004).

Bat tissue, hair, and muscle samples were collected from recovered carcasses as per protocols available from the American Museum of Natural History (2013) to provide a future opportunity to investigate migratory patterns of affected species and confirm identification of species.

## **2.2 SEARCHER EFFICIENCY BIAS TRIALS**

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted to adjust mortality estimates for carcasses missed by surveyors. To achieve a reliable estimate of searcher efficiency, four trials were conducted during the study period (late May – early June, early August, late August – September, and October). Fresh, previously frozen, and discreetly marked bats (n=20) and birds (n=20) were used for the trials. No more than 10 carcasses

were placed at a time to avoid swamping scavengers and overly-altering searchers. Carcasses were placed and re-sighted by an independent third party and were left in place for a period of 14 days to assess scavenger removal (described below). Searcher efficiency was calculated for birds and bats using the method presented in OMNR (2011 _a_ , _b_ ):

## **2.3 CARCASS REMOVAL (SCAVENGER) BIAS TRIALS**

Scavenger removal trials were conducted to adjust mortality estimates for carcasses removed by scavengers prior to being located by searchers. Four scavenger removal trials were conducted concurrently with searcher efficiency trials described above. Fresh, previously frozen and discretely marked carcasses in good condition were used in the scavenger trials. Carcasses were re-sighted approximately every 3 days for a period of 14 days to coincide with search events. A correction factor for scavenger removal was calculated as per OMNR (2011 _a_ , _b_ ):

## **2.4 SEARCH AREA BIAS**

An average of 99.77% (SD=0.44) of the 50 m area around each of the search turbines was searched; as such no correction for individual search plots was applied. Since a subset (40 of 79) of turbines was selected for the monitoring program, a correction factor of 0.51 was applied to adjust the fatality estimates for the total number of turbines across the QWP.

As with year one monitoring (Hemmera 2013), the fatality estimate method provided in the OMNR Guidance documents was used. This method maintains consistency with the recently released Bird Studies Canada (BSC) database template.

## **3.0 RESULTS**

## **3.1 TIMING OF BAT FATALITIES**

The first bat fatality was found on April 22 and the last on September 30, 2014. Bat fatalities, particularly migratory tree bats, exhibited two peaks likely associated with spring and fall migration; migratory tree bats were recovered in every month ( **Figure 2** ).

Silver-haired bat (n=18) was the most abundant species recovered representing approximately 69% of total bat fatalities, and were detected in every month ( **Figure 3** and **Table 1** ). Hoary bats were only detected in July and August, and little brown myotis was detected in May, July, August and September ( **Figure 3** ).

## **3.2 DISTRIBUTION OF BAT FATALITIES**

The number of regularly searched turbines was fairly evenly distributed between the north (n=20) and south (n=23) portions of the Project ( **Figure 4** and **Appendix A** as a series of four figures). Thirteen bat carcasses were recovered in the north portion, and 13 carcasses were recovered in the south portion. Migratory tree bats accounted for 81% (n=21/26) of bat carcasses identified to species group and little brown bats accounted for the remaining 19% (n=5/26). There were no significant differences in total bat fatalities, migratory bat fatalities, or myotis bat fatalities between the north and south portions of the QWP.

Individual turbines with the greatest number of carcass recoveries were T7 and T27 in the north portion of the QWP, each with three bat fatalities, and T56 and T68 in the south portion, each with two bat fatalities ( **Figure 4** ).

## **3.4 DISTRIBUTION OF BIRD FATALITIES**

Bird fatalities were evenly distributed between the north (n=6) and south (n=5) ends of the QWP ( **Figure 8** ). No more than one carcass was recovered from any one turbine. More (8/11) bird fatalities were recovered at turbines with 49 m blades than with 44 m blades; however, this difference was not significant based on a one-way Mann-Whitney test; n=40; df=1; P=0.23).

## **3.5 FATALITY ESTIMATES**

Searcher efficiency was calculated for birds and bats using a total of 40 fresh, previously frozen carcasses (20 birds and 20 bats) during four trial events in May, August (early and late), and October, 2014. Searcher efficiency values were 0.35 for birds and 0.61 for bats. Scavenger removal values were 0.79 for birds and 0.71 for bats. A spreadsheet used to derive searcher efficiency and scavenger removal values is provided as **Appendix B** .

Application of these correction factors to the 11 bird and 26 bat carcasses recovered between April 3 and October 14, 2014 at the QWP yields an estimated 78 birds and 118 bats, or 1.0 birds and 1.5 bats per turbine per year. The assumed species composition represented by the 118 estimated bat fatalities based on recoveries during the monitoring program is weighted toward silver-haired bats ( **Table 4** ).

## **4.0 DISCUSSION**

The following section discusses bat and bird fatality estimates at the QWP and compares the results between the two years of monitoring (2013 – 2014). Additionally the results from the QWP are summarized in relation to other wind energy projects in the Peace Region, Canada, and North America, and compared with fatality thresholds established in other provinces.

## **4.1 BAT FATALITIES**

Bat fatalities at the QWP varied across the two years of monitoring; 4.3 fatalities per turbine in 2013 and 1.5 fatalities per turbine in 2014. These results are generally below calculated national and regional averages; and the thresholds established in other jurisdictions (BC has no established thresholds):

- Bird Studies Canada (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014);

- Peace District Regional Average (Hemmera analysis)

- Proportions of migratory tree bat fatalities North America-wide (Arnett et al. 2008).

- Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources threshold (OMNR 2011 _a_ ).

- Alberta Bat Mitigation Framework for Wind Power Development (Alberta Government (2013)

In 2014, the national Wind Energy Bird and Bat Monitoring Database (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014) was updated to include uncorrected fatalities from 50 post construction monitoring reports in Canada (26 more projects than reported in the 2012 database). In addition to including more operational projects in the database, the updated database now includes corrected mortality estimates from 34 wind projects from 2007 to 2012. Across Canada, a total of 4,020 uncorrected bat fatalities were reported from the 1,376 turbines searched, representing a mean of 2.92 fatalities per turbine. Their regional average annual bat fatality estimates ranged from 0.26 bats/turbine (SD=0.10) in Atlantic Canada; 5.59 bats/turbine (SD=4.73) in Alberta; and 19.08 bats/turbine (SD=2.38) in Ontario (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014). Their analysis did not provide a provincial average for BC.

A regional estimate for the South Peace of 2.0 bats/turbine/year (0.67 bats/MW/year) was derived from the Bear Mountain (unpublished data) and Dokie (Stantec 2012) monitoring data by summing the estimated fatalities at both projects and dividing by the total number of turbines.

A synthesis of bat fatalities at wind energy facilities (Arnett et al. 2008) reports that 80% of total fatalities reported in North America are migratory tree bats. Nationally, 73% of bat fatalities are tree bats (eastern red bat, hoary bat and silver-haired bat) (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014). Approximately 71% of bat fatalities at Dokie were tree bats. The proportion of tree bat fatalities at the QWP was slightly lower than these findings in 2013 (60%, n=31/50[1] ) and slightly higher (81%, n=21/26) in 2014.

The Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (OMNR 2011 _a_ ) significance threshold is 10 bats/turbine/year while the Alberta Government (2013) has established a threshold of 4 – 8 _migratory_ bat species per year. In both jurisdictions exceeding the threshold requires consultation with regulators regarding potential mitigation and further monitoring. After two years of monitoring, the results from QWP are below established thresholds in both jurisdictions for total bat numbers, and for migratory bat fatalities. Based on species composition of recovered carcasses, the QWP estimates for migratory tree bat impacts are 2.6 migratory bats/ turbine/year in 2013 and 1.2 migratory bats/ turbine/year in 2014.

## **4.2 BIRD FATALITIES**

Wind turbines are generally considered to have non-significant effects on local and regional bird populations, with most sites typically averaging three to four fatalities per turbine per year throughout North America (Curry and Kerlinger 2011). A total of 1,744 uncorrected bird fatalities have been reported from the 1,376 turbines searched representing a mean of 1.3 fatalities per turbine across Canada (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014). The average annual bird fatality estimates ranged from 2.35 birds/turbine (SD=1.32) in Alberta; 1.19 birds/turbine (SD=1.12) in Atlantic Canada; and 5.45 birds/turbine (SD=0.76) in Ontario (Bird Studies Canada et al. 2014). Their analysis did not provide a provincial average for BC.

Songbird fatalities were calculated for North American wind energy facilities at 2.10 to 3.35 small birds/MW (Erikson et al. 2014).

A regional (South Peace) estimate of 2.2 bird fatalities/turbine/year was derived from the Bear Mountain and Dokie monitoring data by summing the total fatalities and dividing by the number of turbines.

The QWP estimate of 1.0 bird fatalities/turbine/year, or 0.6 birds/MW/year, for 2014 is below the all of the above average fatality estimates, and the current Peace region estimate based on the two older operating wind projects (Bear Mountain and Dokie). The 2013 estimate of 3.2 bird fatalities/turbine/year was slightly above only the Atlantic Canada average, and above the regional estimate. Both 2013 and 2014 estimates are well below the threshold (14 birds/turbine/year) established in the OMNR (2011 _b_ ) guidelines. To our knowledge, Ontario is the only province to establish a threshold for bird mortality.

## **4.3 FATALITY DISTRIBUTION**

No significant difference in bird, bird groups (songbirds and raptors), or bat fatalities (total and migratory tree vs. other bats) was detected between the north and south portions of the QWP during 2013 and 2014. However, more bird (one-way Mann-Whitney with chi-square approximation; n=80; df=1; P<0.02) and bat (n=80; df=1; P<0.03) fatalities occurred at turbines with 49 m blades than at turbines with 44 m blades (both designs are 95 m at the hub). This finding is somewhat consistent with those of Barclay et al. (2007), who determined that turbine tower height (to top of blades) was strongly correlated with the corrected number of bat fatalities at 21 North American wind energy projects. They did not find a significant relationship between tower height and bird fatalities, or between rotor-swept area and the number of corrected bird or bat fatalities Barclay et al. (2007). The results from the QWP in 2013 and 2014 suggest that the greater rotor swept area and overall turbine height associated with 49 m blades has an effect on both bird and bat fatalities.

## **5.0 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS**

The following section provides conclusions regarding the significance of effects observed as they relate to the EA predictions and the objectives in the monitoring program (Hemmera 2012).

## **5.1 VERIFICATION OF EA PREDICTIONS**

The EA application for the QWP predicted low, non-significant impacts to birds and low to moderate, nonsignificant residual impacts to bats (EPCOR 2009). Based on discussion provided above including the application of available Canadian mortality thresholds (i.e., Alberta Government 2013 and OMNR 2011a, b), the impacts predicted in the EA are considered accurate. As such no additional mitigation actions over and above those designed into the project to reduce effects are required at this time.

## **5.2 MONITORING PROGRAM OBJECTIVES**

The results of the program show the following relationships between turbines and fatalities at the QWP:

- The corrected fatality estimates for birds and bats compare favourably with other wind energy projects operating in North America. See above for more details.

- Songbird, raptor (no fatalities reported), resident bat, and migratory tree bat fatalities are evenly distributed among groups of turbines. More birds and bats, however, were killed by turbines with longer (49 m) blades than by shorter (44 m) blades.

- No turbines experienced mass mortality events, the maximum fatalities at any one turbine through the year was three bats and one bird (turbine 7), and on one day the maximum was three bats (mid-May 2014).

- The EA Application (EPCOR 2009) prediction of non-significant effects was accurate and no follow-up actions to reduce effects are necessary.

## **5.3 RECOMMENDATION**

Capital Power Corp. has completed two years of operational monitoring for bird and bat fatalities at the QWP and has fulfilled the requirements under EAC commitment 5.7.7 (#E10-01, June 2010). Unless otherwise required by the responsible regulatory agencies, no further bird and bat fatality monitoring is being recommended.
